title: How much do cash transfers improve nutrition?
summary: New research on Kenya finds that cash transfers increase how much very poor households in rural areas spend on food. The response is larger than most previous studies have found, yet the increase is smaller than conventional 'correlational' methods would suggest.

title: Can countries cut air pollution without hurting economic growth?
summary: Air pollution kills more people than AIDS or terrorism, but new economic research shows that democracies like India can cut it substantially through cheap, automated emissions markets rather than costly quick-fix technologies.

title: How becoming a regional capital redirects urban growth
summary: New research using hundreds of administrative reforms worldwide shows that cities that become regional capitals grow faster, especially where political status and market access reinforce one another.

title: Pairing cash transfers with behaviour change meaningfully improves child nutrition
summary: Pairing peer-led nutrition behaviour-change groups with ongoing cash transfers substantially improved children's diets and development, but meaningful reductions in stunting required combining cash with a larger one-time livelihoods grant.

title: Why workers avoid unfamiliar neighbourhoods – and how one visit can help eliminate fears
summary: A field experiment with casual workers in Nairobi finds that people are reluctant to work in unfamiliar parts of their own city. A single visit to an unfamiliar neighbourhood is enough to eliminate this aversion.

title: Caste, race, and power: The barriers to political inclusion
summary: A review of research into marginalised 'subaltern' groups across the Global South examines why democratic gains for the poor and excluded have proved so difficult to secure – and why, in many places, they are now being reversed.

title: Why digital tools alone won't close the gender employment gap
summary: Digital tools like apps and online platforms are often promoted as a way to expand women's economic opportunities, but access alone rarely translates into lasting engagement or economic gains. The most effective interventions are those designed around women's specific constraint…

title: AI RCTs are booming – to be useful they must evolve
summary: AI RCTs are on the rise; a trend that’s set to continue, and is likely to intensify. But randomising a rapidly evolving, increasingly widely adopted, technology poses a distinct set of challenges. So how can we actually garner durable, generalisable and policy relevant insights?

title: Can workers be trained to be more conscientious, and does it pay off?
summary: A light-touch training programme that helped low-skilled workers in Senegal act more conscientiously boosted their job retention and earnings.

title: Why is political polarisation rising – and can we stop it?
summary: Political polarisation is rising worldwide and carries especially high costs in developing countries, but research points to evidence-based interventions – from cross-partisan media exposure to identity priming – that can help build community resilience against it.

title: The progress paradox: When female authority deepens the gender divide
summary: In Lebanon, being randomly assigned a female academic advisor makes women hold more egalitarian gender views decades later, while pushing men towards more conservative ones – widening the gender divide, especially in male-dominated fields and among religious students.
